04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The external drive was smaller than Emma remembered. She turned it over in her palm, examining the scratched black casing and the faded strip of tape on which she had written Glenarraidh, 2011. Fifteen years had passed, yet the handwriting belonged unmistakably to the young reporter who had believed that keeping copies of everything was the same as understanding what mattered.

The flat was quiet except for the rain against the window. Emma had promised herself she would sleep, yet she had cleared the kitchen table and made coffee she did not want. The letter lay beside her notebook. Every few minutes her eyes returned to the same line: You were looking in the wrong place.

She connected it to her laptop. For several seconds, nothing happened. Then a small light blinked and a familiar folder appeared.

There were photographs of the town square, recordings of interviews and drafts with names that had ceased to mean anything. Emma opened a document headed Morrison — background. The first page contained the details she already knew: Claire's volunteer work, her disappearance, the appeals issued by her family. The second was a list of people who had agreed to speak to Emma off the record.

The archive had the untidy logic of a young reporter's first serious assignment. Some files were labelled carefully; others were called final, final2 and final-really. Emma almost smiled. Then she noticed that the same rumour appeared in several documents without a clear source. Repetition was not corroboration.

She stopped at the final entry.

Foundation — financial concerns. Source requests anonymity.

No name. No telephone number. Only a date and a reference to an email she had received the morning after Claire was reported missing.

Emma searched the archive. The email was there, preserved as a PDF, with its sender's address concealed in the copy she had made for her editor. The message claimed that Claire had been under personal pressure and might have wanted to leave Glenarraidh. It offered no evidence. Emma had nevertheless used it to shape her article.

She remembered a newsroom deadline and an editor asking for something beyond another appeal for information. The pressure was real. So was her decision to rely on a claim she had not checked. She could explain how it happened without excusing it.

She read the paragraph twice, feeling the old embarrassment settle into something more precise. It was not merely that the information had been unreliable. She had allowed an anonymous allegation to become the explanation readers remembered.

On the screen, a note in her own handwriting appeared beside the email: Check with trust. Ask about grants.

She had never followed it up.

A message from Sarah appeared on her phone. Are you still awake? Don't publish anything about the letter until we talk.

Emma typed Of course, then deleted it. She had no intention of publishing. Not yet.

Instead, she opened the foundation's archived website and began looking for the grants promised to students in 2011.
